title: Church segregation, Plessy, learning by ear and playing the picture show
summary: Segregated church pews, Catholic schools closed to Black children, then self-taught piano and playing for silent films in Covington theaters.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: I can bum a ride with you.

Yes, that's right, yes, we have, right on the corner, that particular, right across from McDonough 6 school, and the Bowmans always had pews way up in front of the church, but when Papa, Mama married Papa, he was dark, brown skinned, and the ushers would, came up to Papa, and asked him to please be seated in the rear of the church, because that they had reservations for colored people to sit in the back of the church, that time they had a little sign for colored only, back there, see, for colored patrons only. So, Mama said, you sit right here, and they said he came back two, three times, and so Papa, Mama said, don't you move, you stay right here, because that was the family pew up there, two, three of them, two peributes, and so, he didn't move, so, after that, they got, after church was over, he came up to Papa, and he says, said something about, he shouldn't sit in that part of the church before, again, because that was reserved for whites, and so, they took Grandpa and his family, just for whites, they'd understood that's where it was, and so Mama decided from then on, she didn't want to go to church anymore, she, although we were Catholic, and we were born Catholic, we were trade men, and not until she went to California did she start to go into church again, because the same thing happened in Covington, the same thing, because of the fact they isolated the Catholics to the the fact that they would, the colors would sit in the back, and but the communion time, you could go up together, and sit after the, after the whites people had received communion, and this was something, in those days, it doesn't happen today, you understand, but this thing there, they, and after they received communion, you would receive communion, that was something that the church itself tolerated because of the law, you see, and that they, while the church, they closed the church down, and that's one of the reasons why the church was a fear for the law, closing down the church, so there was, so, I mean, the church was fearful of the law, closing down, so they, they had to abide by that law, so from two later years, when they fought that off, but there's a religion, there's Catholic, that's what was, and did you ever go to a Catholic school? No, I, I went to, in Covington, in Covington, no, there wasn't any, you see, there never was, at that time, the Catholics did not take in any, uh, color that told at that time, they didn't take anybody in there, other than, uh, they, in fact, they had a school for girls, uh, but it was only for, uh, white girls, and so forth, but not for colored black girls, or anything like that, they, at that time, that was way back now, you ever say, way back in, when segregation was, was tolerated, and so forth, you know, times of the day. Oh, yeah. See, that was, I remember. This was way back in the old days, but it took, uh, it got to change, the church changed all that, you know, as time went on, and of course, it's, uh, the laws became, uh, you know, different, at least all this, uh, the, uh, civil rights, and so forth, movement, so forth, changed, all these things, and everything opened up, and it's changed everything, but, but, uh, no one could fight that law, because it's separate, but equal, because it was definitely something that, uh, in fact, it happened during the time, uh, right on the New Orleans Great Northern train going to Covington, you see, Plessy versus New Orleans Great, huh? Ferguson, Plessy, was it Plessy? Plessy versus Ferguson, I remember it. Ferguson, yeah, yeah, yeah. On the New Orleans Great Northern, on the New Orleans Great Northern Red Road. I don't remember it too well. The judge in the Supreme Court, as a separate but equal would be all right, and that's what, until that was, uh, outlawed, and voted down in the Supreme Court years later. What, did you get any musical training in Covington? Well, my mother, I just took the musical, and played by ear, played by ear, and, uh, played by ear, but I was good at it. You see, when you play by ear, it's just like Cookie did. You go, you get out and you can develop well, it's like a lot of the jazz musicians today. You play by ear, you, you, you can do a lot of things that you invent, you see, it have to be a composing in years to come. So, uh, I would play piano, and make up the songs, and, as I heard them, uh, uh, played around, or, you know, records, and you'd hear them blasting out of people's houses. You can hear records in those old days, Mamie Smith records, and you could hear all the old, Tony O'Neill, Ted Lewis records, you know. You could hear all the old, you could hear all the, you could hear all the, you could hear all the, you could hear that same tune all day. So that you'd learn it, and eventually play it. See, I never bought any, because I'd just listen, and then I learned how to play it. But it was soon, so then I got a job playing at the theater, at the colored picture show, because the guy played down there, he played down there. He played nothing but boogie woogie all through the love scenes. So they didn't want him in there, because he messed up the love scenes with boogie woogie. That's all he played stuff with boogie woogie. That's all he played. So they say Doc played a little different stuff with stuff I was composing, didn't know it. Horses would bloom, so I'd make some kind of horse music. If there was anything, they were shooting at one another, I'd make some kind of a, you know, sort of a radical sort of a overture or something, like it was going to have a war going on, and I would do it with my, just originally. But the funniest thing that I had noticed, they would sometimes, when they'd come down to the color house, they'd bring the fourth reel first, you see, then they'd start to come back again. They couldn't let them have the other reel, so they'd send the second reel. Now you have to put that together, what the story was about, because they started with the fourth reel, now it's the second reel, then they come back with the fifth reel, that five reels, you know, then you come back maybe with the third reel, and then the first reel, and you put it all together, and you figure out what kind of show. But so that's what, so one time, it was there, and the old guys, the films caught on fire, and you see what I mean, and the, and the guys had buckets of water was coming in, and put the film out, they couldn't get the film back to the white picture show, because they'd switch them, see, the same guy, finally, owned the white picture show, and the black picture show. So he was sending one film down there, while he'd pick up the other one, bring them down there, and he had them switching, so he could have one film playing two houses. And that's what happened. And later on he gave me a, he said, what do you call it, I got transferred to the other theater, and then they paid me a dollar more a week, to the white theater, until it came the four horsemen of the apocalypse, I think it was, and they had the music with it, had to read. I couldn't read that hard music that came with the score, and so, and so they had to finally get some piano player from Yale to play the piano, for the score that was, that hard score that was coming. That was changing, and coming in sound was coming. But that's why I got a lot of experience in writing, and making up songs, and might have helped me later on in the poetry.
